statements.text: A toddler was seen flailing in a shallow pond, unable to keep her head above water for more than a few seconds at a time.
The pond was only about knee-deep and children sometimes play there on hot days.
There was no parent or babysitter around when the toddler was struggling in the pond.
Wading into the pond to save the child was easy and safe but would ruin new shoes and get clothes wet and muddy.
The person who saves the child would be late for work after handing the child over and changing clothes.
Students in a Practical Ethics course generally agree that one should save the child despite minor inconveniences.
The story of the drowning child was first told in the article 'Famine, Affluence and Morality' published in 1972.
In 2011, a 2-year-old girl named Wang Yue was hit by a van in Foshan, China, and left bleeding in the street.
Eighteen people walked or rode past Wang Yue without stopping to help, often averting their gaze.
A second van ran over Wang Yue's leg before a street cleaner raised the alarm.
Wang Yue was rushed to hospital but died.
In 2017, 5.4 million children under 5 years old died, mostly from preventable or treatable causes.
A man in Ghana described a small boy who died of measles because his parents had no money for hospital treatment.
Many children die from measles, malaria, and diarrhea due to lack of safe drinking water, sanitation, and medical treatment.
Organizations like Oxfam, Against Malaria Foundation, and Evidence Action work to reduce poverty and provide mosquito nets and safe drinking water.
These organizations are reducing child mortality, and more funding would allow them to save more lives.
Donating a relatively small amount of money can save a child's life.
People often spend money on non-essential items like drinks, meals out, clothing, movies, concerts, vacations, new cars, or house renovations.
Choosing to spend money on non-essential items instead of effective charities may result in leaving a child to die.
The proportion of the world's population living in extreme poverty fell from 34% in 1993 to 10.7% in 2013 according to the World Bank.
This reduction in extreme poverty is one of the greatest achievements in human history.
Only 7% of people surveyed worldwide answered correctly that extreme poverty had almost halved in the last 20 years.
In the United States, 19 out of 20 people surveyed falsely believed that extreme poverty had not changed or had increased.
Almost all children worldwide are vaccinated today, with about 80% of 1-year-old children vaccinated against some disease.
Only 13% of people surveyed were aware of the high global vaccination rates.
Most people incorrectly believe the majority of the world's population lives in low-income or high-income countries.
Three-quarters of the world's population live in middle-income countries.
91% of the world's population lives in middle-income or high-income countries.
Only 9% of the world's population lives in low-income countries.
Not all people living in low-income countries are in extreme poverty.
Large middle-income countries such as India and Nigeria have very unequal income distributions.
Many millions of people in India and Nigeria live in extreme poverty.
Many people do not give to charities that seek to reduce extreme poverty because they believe it is a hopeless task.
It is vital that more people learn about the impressive progress in reducing extreme poverty.
It is essential to listen to people living in extreme poverty to understand their experiences and what they want to change.
The World Bank asked researchers to document the experiences of 60,000 women and men in 73 countries.
Poor people reported being short of food for all or part of the year, often eating only one meal per day.
Poor people sometimes have to choose between feeding their children or themselves.
Poor people sometimes cannot feed themselves or their children adequately.
Poor people cannot save money and may have to borrow from local moneylenders with high interest.
Debt from borrowing can continue to mount, making it difficult to become free of it.
Poor people cannot afford to send their children to school or must take them out if the harvest is poor.
Poor people live in unstable houses made with mud or thatch that need rebuilding every two or three years or after severe weather.
Poor people have no nearby source of safe drinking water and must carry water long distances.
Water carried by poor people can make them ill unless it is boiled.
Extreme poverty is often accompanied by a degrading state of powerlessness.
Even in democracies, poor people may have to accept humiliation without protest.
Police may not listen to complaints from poor people if someone takes what little they have.
The law may not protect poor people from rape or sexual harassment.
Poor people have a pervading sense of shame and failure because they cannot provide for their children.
Poverty traps people and causes them to lose hope of escaping a life of hard work with nothing to show beyond survival.
The World Bank defines extreme poverty as not having enough income to meet basic human needs for food, water, shelter, clothing, sanitation, health care, and education.
Between 1990 and 2015, more than a billion people lifted themselves out of extreme poverty.
The global poverty rate is now lower than it has ever been in recorded history.
As of the most recent data, 736 million people still live on less than $1.90 a day.
The $1.90 a day figure is the global extreme poverty line set by the World Bank.
The World Bank adjusts the $1.90 figure for purchasing power parity to compare goods and services across countries.
In wealthy societies, most poverty is relative, with people feeling poor because they cannot afford advertised goods but still owning items like televisions.
In the United States, 97% of those classified as poor own a color TV.
Three quarters of poor people in the United States own a car.
Three quarters of poor people in the United States have air conditioning.
The 736 million people living in extreme poverty are poor by an absolute standard tied to basic human needs.
People in extreme poverty are likely to be hungry for at least part of each year.
Even if they get enough food, people in extreme poverty are probably malnourished due to lack of essential nutrients.
Malnutrition in children stunts growth and can cause permanent brain damage.
Poor people may not be able to afford to send their children to school.
Basic and life-saving health care services are usually beyond the means of people living in extreme poverty.
The extreme poverty rate in East Asia and the Pacific dropped from 60% in 1990 to 2.3% in 2015.
Nearly 10 million extremely poor people remain in China as of 2015.
Smaller numbers of extremely poor people remain elsewhere in the East Asia and Pacific region.
The World Bank's 2018 report on poverty stated that from 1990 to 2015, the percentage of the world's population living in extreme poverty dropped from nearly 36% to 10%.
The global extreme poverty rate dropped by an average of one percentage point per year from 1990 to 2015.
Between 2013 and 2015, the global extreme poverty rate dropped by only one percentage point.
Progress in reducing poverty is slower in sub-Saharan Africa than in Asia.
Sub-Saharan Africa is the region with the highest proportion of people living in extreme poverty, with about 4 in every 10 people affected.
The World Bank reports that extreme poverty is increasingly becoming a Sub-Saharan African problem.
Of the world's 28 poorest countries, 27 are in Sub-Saharan Africa, all with poverty rates above 30 percent.
The Brookings Institution stated that by 2023, Africa's share of the world's extremely poor will rise to over 80 percent, up from 60 percent in 2016.
To end poverty by 2030, Africa would need more than one person to escape poverty every second, but currently Africa adds poor people.
In September 2018, more than half of all humans alive were middle-class or above, using a definition that includes the ability to afford leisure and consumer goods.
About 3.8 billion people today live at a level of affluence never previously known except in the courts of kings and nobles.
Louis XIV could not keep Versailles cool in summer as effectively as most people in high-income nations can keep their homes cool today.
Louis XIV's gardeners could not produce the variety of fresh fruits and vegetables available year-round today.
Medical care available to Louis XIV would be considered inadequate by today's standards.
People today are much better off than their own great-grandparents.
People today can expect to live about 30 years longer than a century ago.
A century ago, 1 child in 10 died in infancy.
In most rich nations today, less than 1 in 200 children die in infancy.
Americans today spend, on average, only 6.4% of their income on buying food.
If Americans work a 40-hour week, it takes them barely two hours to earn enough to feed themselves for the week.
This leaves Americans with more money to spend on consumer goods, entertainment, and vacations.
In 2019, Forbes calculated that there were 2,153 billionaires in the world.
The number of billionaires in the world nearly doubled in ten years.
Billionaires keep getting richer, widening the gap between themselves and ordinary wage earners.
In December 2018, Boeing Business Jets launched the BBJ 777X, a new model based on the Boeing 777.
The BBJ 777X can fly more than halfway around the world without stopping.
The price of a 'green' BBJ 777X aircraft is $450 million.
A 'green' aircraft refers to a plane without the interior fitting.
Adding the interior to the BBJ 777X costs another $25–$50 million.
In commercial service, the BBJ 777X seats 365 passengers.
The private version of the BBJ 777X might carry 35 people.
Owning a large airplane carrying a small number of people maximizes personal contribution to global warming.
Superyachts are considered a conspicuous waste of money and resources.
Business Insider reported in 2017 that it has become normal for the world's wealthiest individuals to spend millions or billions on superyachts.
Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan owns Azzam, the largest private yacht at 180 meters long.
Azzam edged out Eclipse, previously the largest yacht, owned by Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich.
Azzam is estimated to have cost $400 million and has accommodation for 36 guests.
Americans bought 13.7 billion gallons of bottled water in 2017.
Making coffee at home costs pennies compared to spending four dollars or more on a latte.
People sometimes order a second soda or glass of wine at a restaurant and do not finish it.
Dr. Timothy Jones led a U.S. government–funded study of food waste.
Dr. Timothy Jones found that 14% of household garbage is perfectly good food in its original packaging and not out of date.
More than half of the wasted food found by Dr. Jones was dry-packaged or canned goods that keep for a long time.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that Americans waste 30–40% of their food supply.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture values the wasted food at about $161 billion.
A survey found that people in the United Kingdom buy on average £200 worth of clothing per person that they never wear.
Fashion designer Deborah Lindquist claims that the average woman in the United States owns more than $600 worth of clothing not worn in the last year.
The text asserts that almost all people, men and women alike, buy things they do not need, some of which they never use.
Most people believe they would not hesitate to save a drowning child, even at considerable cost to themselves.
Thousands of children die each day while people spend money on things they take for granted.
Bob is close to retirement and has invested most of his savings in a rare and valuable old car, a Bugatti, which he has not insured.
Bob derives pleasure from his Bugatti and expects to sell it for a comfortable retirement.
Bob sees a runaway train heading toward a child playing on the tracks.
Bob can throw a switch to divert the train onto a siding where his Bugatti is parked, which would destroy the car but save the child.
Bob decides not to throw the switch, prioritizing his car over the child's safety.
Philosopher Peter Unger developed the Bugatti story as a variation on the drowning child scenario.
Unger’s story introduces uncertainty about the outcome of sacrifice, as Bob cannot be certain the child will die if he does nothing.
People often doubt whether their charitable donations really help the intended recipients.
Most people respond that Bob acted badly by not sacrificing his car to save the child.
The implication is drawn that saving money for retirement could be seen as refusing to use that money to help save lives.
Another example by Unger involves a hiker with a seriously injured leg asking for a ride to the hospital.
If the driver refuses to help the hiker, the hiker may lose his leg.
If the driver helps, the hiker is likely to bleed onto the recently restored white leather seats.
Most people respond that the driver should take the hiker to the hospital, even at the cost of damaging the car.
The text suggests that people consider it obligatory to lessen the serious suffering of innocent others at some cost to themselves.
The text states that our moral intuitions are not always reliable.
The text presents a logical argument for helping those in extreme poverty.
The first premise of the argument is that suffering and death from lack of food, shelter, and medical care are bad.
The second premise is that if it is in your power to prevent something bad from happening without sacrificing anything nearly as important, it is wrong not to do so.
The third premise is that by donating to effective charities, you can prevent suffering and death from lack of food, shelter, and medical care, without sacrificing anything nearly as important.
The conclusion is that if you do not donate to effective charities, you are doing something wrong.
The drowning-child story is used as an application of the argument for donating.
Ruining shoes and being late for work are not as important as the life of a child.
Reupholstering a car is not as significant as losing a leg.
The text claims it would be a stretch to suggest that the loss of a car rivals the significance of the death of an innocent person.
Children often die from the condition described in the text.
The condition would be curable if the parents could afford to take their child to a hospital.
Parents in such circumstances would give up almost anything to ensure their child's survival.
Thinking ethically involves putting yourself in the place of others, such as the parents or the child.
The Golden Rule is stated as 'Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.'
The Golden Rule is best known to most westerners from the words of Jesus as reported by Matthew and Luke.
The Golden Rule is older and more universal than its Christian formulation.
The Golden Rule is prominent in the teachings of Buddhism, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, and Jainism.
The Golden Rule is found in Leviticus and was later emphasized by the sage Hillel in Judaism.
The Golden Rule requires us to accept that the desires of others ought to count as if they were our own.
If we think ethically, the suffering and death of a child must count as if it were our own.
The second premise allows for exceptions when preventing something bad would require risking something nearly as important.
If preventing the deaths of other children would require neglecting your own children, the second premise does not require you to act.
'Nearly as important' is a deliberately vague term in the argument.
The author trusts the reader to be honest with themselves about what is as important as saving a life.
Analogies and stories can be pushed too far.
Rescuing a child drowning in front of you is different from donating to help people who are far away.
The argument presented appeals to reason and an abstract moral principle rather than emotion.
To reject the argument, one must find a flaw in the reasoning.
The argument states that we should donate to aid people in extreme poverty when we can prevent suffering and death without giving up anything nearly as important.
Taking the argument seriously would dramatically change our lives.
The cost of saving one child's life by contributing to an effective non-profit may not be great.
After saving one child, there remain more children in need who can be saved at a relatively small additional cost.
A $200 donation to the Against Malaria Foundation enables the purchase of 100 long-lasting insecticidal nets.
100 long-lasting insecticidal nets will protect about 180 people from malaria-carrying mosquitoes.
Malaria in low-income tropical countries is a major cause of children dying.
Malaria, even when not fatal, causes high fever and long-term, debilitating illness.
The author suggests continuing to cut back on unnecessary spending and donating the savings until further giving would sacrifice something nearly as important as preventing malaria.

We tend to assume that if people do not harm others, keep promises, do not lie or cheat, support their children and elderly parents, and contribute a little to their local community, they have done well.
If we have money left over after meeting our needs and those of our dependents, we may spend it as we please.
Giving to strangers, especially those beyond one's community, is not generally considered something we have to do.
If the basic argument is right, then what many consider acceptable behavior must be viewed in a new, more ominous light.
Spending surplus money on concerts, fashionable shoes, fine dining, good wines, or holidays in faraway lands is described as doing something wrong if the argument is accepted.
The three premises of the argument become harder to accept when their demanding implications are considered.
The text references the Gospels, where Jesus told the rich man to sell his possessions and give to the poor.
Jesus said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.
Jesus praised the Good Samaritan who helped a stranger.
Jesus urged those who give feasts to invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind.
Jesus said that God will save those who have fed the hungry, given drink to the thirsty, and clothed the naked.
Jesus placed more emphasis on charity for the poor than on anything else.
The early Christian community in Jerusalem sold all their possessions and divided them according to need.
The Franciscans, an order of monks founded by Francis of Assisi, took a vow of poverty and renounced all private property.
Thomas Aquinas wrote that whatever we have in superabundance is owed, of natural right, to the poor for their sustenance.
Aquinas quoted Ambrose and the Decretum Gratiani in support of the view that surplus wealth belongs to the poor.

The Decretum Gratiani states: 'The bread which you withhold belongs to the hungry: the clothing you shut away, to the naked: and the money you bury in the earth is the redemption and freedom of the penniless.'
For these Christians, sharing surplus wealth with the poor is considered a duty and the poor's right, not merely charity.
Aquinas stated that it is not theft to take and use another's property in a case of extreme need, as it becomes the taker's property by reason of that need.
John Locke wrote that charity gives every man a title to so much out of another's plenty as will keep him from extreme want, where he has no means to subsist otherwise.
Jim Wallis, founder and editor of Sojourners, points out that the Bible contains more than 3,000 references to alleviating poverty.
Jim Wallis believes the large number of biblical references to poverty is reason to make it a central moral issue for Christians.
Rick Warren, author and pastor, visited a small church in South Africa in 2003 that sheltered 25 children orphaned by AIDS.
Rick Warren said the small church was doing more for the poor than his entire megachurch.
Rick Warren stated that his only interest is to get people to care about places like Darfur and Rwanda.
In Judaism, the Hebrew word for 'charity,' tzedakah, means 'justice.'
For Jews, giving to the poor is considered an essential part of living a just life.
The Talmud says that charity is equal in importance to all the other commandments combined.
The Talmud states that Jews should give at least 10% of their income as tzedakah.
Islam requires adherents to help those in need.
Muslims above a minimum level of wealth must give zakat in proportion to their assets each year.
For gold and silver, which today includes cash and other liquid assets, Muslims are required to give 2.5% every year as zakat.
Muslims may also give sadaqa, which can include both money and labor.
Sadaqa is optional, unlike zakat.
Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are related traditions with roots in the same part of the world.
The Chinese tradition is said to focus more on how one acts toward those with whom one has a relationship, especially family, than on charity toward strangers.
Mencius is regarded as the most authoritative interpreter of the Confucian tradition after Confucius.
A work describing Mencius's teachings recounts his visit to the court of King Hui of Liang.
Mencius told King Hui that not issuing stores of granaries to people dying from famine is like stabbing a man and blaming the weapon.
The idea that we have a strong moral obligation to help those in need is not new.
In one-on-one situations where rescue is easy, people generally feel it would be wrong not to help.
Most people fail to act on appeals to help those living in extreme poverty in the world's poorest countries.
Most Americans consider themselves charitable.
Americans donated $427 billion to charities in 2018, with 68% coming directly from individuals.
Charitable giving in the United States is around 2% of the U.S. gross national income.
The U.S. charitable giving figure is boosted by substantial giving from a small number of extremely wealthy people.
The United States ranks 12th in the percentage of the population that gives to charity, with 61% giving.
Myanmar ranks first in the percentage of the population that gives to charity, with 88% giving.
The Charities Aid Foundation assesses country generosity by looking at helping a stranger, volunteering time, and donating money.
In 2018, Indonesia ranked first in overall generosity, ahead of Australia and New Zealand.
In 2018, the United States ranked fourth in overall generosity, followed by Ireland and the United Kingdom.
According to Giving USA 2019, the largest portion of money Americans give—29%—goes to religious institutions.
Missions, both domestic and international, may provide aid in addition to seeking converts.
Aid for developing countries is likely to be only a fraction of the 5% of the total amount donated to religious institutions.
The next biggest sector for charitable giving is education, including universities, colleges, and libraries.
A small percentage of educational giving goes toward scholarships to students from low-income countries or to fund research that can help reduce poverty and disease in those countries.
Giving USA 2019 lumps donations to international aid organizations together with gifts to other organizations that do not give aid to the poor.
Some organizations included in this category run international exchange programs or do work for international peace and security.
The entire category of international aid and related organizations received only 5% of all U.S. charitable giving.
This 5% figure was down from the previous year and amounted to less than $23 billion.
Many people who read the book are likely to give to charity or volunteer in their community.
Many people are less inclined to give a substantial portion of their income to save the lives of those living in extreme poverty in faraway places.
The saying 'charity begins at home' reflects the tendency for many people to focus their charitable giving locally.
Some people express resistance to giving to charity in various ways, including in columns, letters, and blogs.
Scott Seider, then a graduate student at Harvard University, interviewed 38 students in two sections of a course at Glennview High and read their papers.
The students at Glennview High were given an article written for The New York Times in 1999 as part of their course reading.
Kathryn, a Glennview student, believes there is no black and white universal code for everyone regarding giving to charity.
Kathryn thinks it is better to accept that everyone has a different view on the issue and is entitled to follow their own beliefs.
The text argues that moral relativism is a position many find attractive until faced with someone doing something clearly wrong.
The text gives an example of someone being cruel to a cat and argues that people do not simply accept such behavior as a matter of personal belief.
The text states that people try to stop those who are cruel to animals, rapists, racists, and terrorists.
Douglas, another Glennview student, objected that the author should not have the right to tell people what to do.
The author acknowledges having no authority over Douglas or the reader.
The author claims the right of free speech to offer arguments for consideration.
Lucy, another Glennview High student, wrote that people who work for their money have the right to spend it on themselves.
Lucy believes that if someone wants to buy a new car, redecorate their house, or get a suit, they should do so.
A critical review on Amazon questioned whether people who spend money on themselves instead of helping those in need are inherently terrible or neglectful citizens.
The author states that they never said people who spend money on themselves are inherently terrible.
The text suggests that middle-class people in developed countries are privileged to be born into social and economic circumstances that allow for a comfortable standard of living.
In other places, people might end up poor no matter how hard they work.
Warren Buffett said that his talent for picking stocks would not produce much if he were in the wrong kind of environment, such as Bangladesh or Peru.
Herbert Simon estimated that 'social capital' is responsible for at least 90% of what people earn in wealthy societies.
Simon defined social capital as living in a society with good institutions, such as an efficient banking system, a police force, and courts.
Infrastructure like roads, communications, and a reliable power supply is also considered part of social capital.
Without social capital, people will struggle to escape poverty, no matter how hard they work.
The text claims that most of the poor work at least as hard as people in wealthy societies.
Work in poor countries is more likely to involve hard physical labor because there are fewer machines to do the jobs.
Occupational health and safety regulations, if they exist in poor countries, are unlikely to be enforced.
Unemployment is higher in poor nations than in rich ones.
Higher unemployment in poor nations is not the fault of the poor.
People have a right to spend the money they earn on themselves.
Having a right to do something does not settle the question of what you should do.
If you have a right to do something, others cannot justifiably force you not to do it.
It is possible to have a right to do something and still be criticized for doing it.
You may have a right to spend your weekend playing video games, but it can still be true that you ought to visit your sick mother.
The rich have a right to spend their money on yachts, large houses, or even to waste it.
People with more modest means should not be forced to forgo less-expensive pleasures that offer relief from work.
It is possible to think that choosing to spend money on luxuries rather than saving human lives is wrong.
There is no contradiction between believing people have a right to spend their money as they choose and believing it is wrong to spend it selfishly.
A right to do as we wish with our money would provide a basis for objecting to forcing the rich to give their money away or to taking it by taxation.
The author is not arguing for higher taxation or coercive means of increasing support for people living in extreme poverty.
The author is discussing what individuals should choose to do with their money to live ethically.
Whether governments should play a role in reducing global poverty is a separate question from the author's argument.
The author's aim is to convince individual readers that they can and should do more to help the poor.
Libertarians resist the idea that we have a duty to help others.
Canadian philosopher Jan Narveson states that we are responsible for evils we inflict on others and owe them compensation.
Jan Narveson claims there is no plausible argument that we owe something as a general duty to those to whom we have done nothing wrong.
The political philosophy of 'You leave me alone, and I'll leave you alone' appeals to the frontier mentality.
There is a callous side to a philosophy that denies responsibilities to those in need through no fault of their own.
Taking libertarianism seriously would require abolishing all state-supported welfare programs for those who can't get a job, are ill, or disabled.
Taking libertarianism seriously would require abolishing all state-funded health care for the aged and those too poor to pay for their own health insurance.
Few people really support such extreme libertarian views.
Most people think we have obligations to those we can help with relatively little sacrifice, especially those in our own country.
If we have caused the poverty of the world's poorest people, even libertarians like Narveson would agree we ought to compensate them.
Some people imagine the world's wealth is a static quantity, like a pie to be divided among people.
In the static wealth model, the bigger the slice the rich get, the less there is for the poor.
1% of the world's people own 45% of the world's wealth.
Less than 10% of the world's people own 84% of the world's wealth.
64% of the world's people own only 2% of the world's wealth.
A 2019 Oxfam report claims the world's 26 richest people own as much as the poorest 50% of the global population.
The concentration of wealth in a few hands is increasing.
Two years before 2019, it took 61 of the world's richest people to own as much as the poorest 50%.
The world's wealth is not fixed in size and is vastly richer now than 1,000 years ago.
Entrepreneurs make themselves rich by finding better ways to create what people want, but they do not necessarily make others poorer.
Extreme poverty means not having enough to meet your basic needs and those of your dependents.
The unequal distribution of the world's wealth is not sufficient to show that the accumulation of immense wealth by a few billionaires has harmed the poor.
Damaging the coral reefs where fish breed has caused a major protein source for poor people to dwindle.
People who used to make a living fishing are now unemployed or have turned to hunting dolphins and whales, including endangered species.
A study estimated that illegal industrial fishing trawlers take $300 million worth of fish out of Senegalese waters alone.
The total value of fish taken by illegal industrial fishing trawlers from West Africa is estimated at $1.3 billion.
The problem of illegal industrial fishing is repeated in many other coastal areas around the world.
President Yoweri Museveni of Uganda accused industrialized countries of causing global warming and harming Africa.
Nearly half of the greenhouse gases now in the atmosphere have come from the United States and Europe.
Without those greenhouse gases, there would be no human-induced global warming problem.
Africa's contribution to global emissions from burning fuel since 1751 is less than 3%.

Africa's contribution to global emissions is somewhat more if land clearing and methane emissions from livestock production are included, but still a small fraction compared to industrialized nations.
The hardship from climate change will fall disproportionately on the poor in regions closer to the equator.
The International Monetary Fund estimated that for a country with an average annual temperature of 25°C, a 1°C increase in temperature would reduce per capita output by up to 1.5%.
This reduction in per capita output from temperature increase will not apply to Europe, the United States, Canada, and other older industrialized nations with much lower average temperatures.
Some scientists believe that precipitation will decrease nearer the equator and increase nearer the poles.
Rainfall upon which hundreds of millions rely to grow their food will become less reliable.
Poor nations depend on agriculture to a far greater degree than rich nations.
In the United States, farm output is only about 1% of the economy.
In Sierra Leone, farm output is 60% of the economy.
In Malawi, 80% of the population are small-scale farmers, virtually all of whom are dependent on rainfall.
Residents of Ghoramara Island in the Bay of Bengal are already seeking resettlement due to rising sea levels causing flooding and salinity.
Densely settled delta regions in Egypt, Bangladesh, India, and Vietnam are especially vulnerable to inundation from small increases in sea level.
Small Pacific Island nations consisting of low-lying coral atolls, like Kiribati and Tuvalu, are in danger of being submerged.
It seems inevitable that in a few decades, small Pacific Island nations like Kiribati and Tuvalu will be submerged.
The greenhouse gas emissions of industrialized nations have harmed, and are continuing to harm, many of the world's poorest people.
The International Monetary Fund has estimated that developing economies will need climate adaptation investment of $80 billion a year until 2050.
In 2014, only $9.3 billion was being invested for climate adaptation in developing economies.
The International Monetary Fund stated that there is some appeal in linking climate finance donations from advanced economies to their contribution to climate change.
The industrialized nations have harmed, and are continuing to harm, the poorer and more vulnerable nations.
In a world with no more capacity to absorb greenhouse gases without damaging climate change, the philosophy of 'You leave me alone, and I'll leave you alone' is almost impossible to live by.
Ceasing to put any more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere is required to truly leave others alone.
The United States government is already giving more than its share of foreign aid, paid for through taxes.
When Americans are asked about U.S. foreign aid as a percentage of income compared to other wealthy countries, only 1 in 20 gives the correct answer.
In 2018, Turkey and Sweden were the most generous nations, both giving more than 1% of their gross national income as foreign aid.
Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, Norway, Denmark, and the United Kingdom also met or exceeded the United Nations target of 0.7% of their national income for foreign aid.
The average among all donor members of the OECD that give foreign aid was 0.38% of gross national income in 2018.
The United States gave just 0.17% of its gross national income as foreign aid in 2018.
The U.S. foreign aid percentage was on a par with Portugal, below France, Italy, Japan, and Spain, and only above countries much less wealthy like Greece, Poland, Hungary, and Russia.
In U.S. politics, it is often assumed that there is little support for foreign aid.
Surveys have frequently found that as many as 7 out of 10 Americans in earlier decades said the U.S. spends 'too much' on foreign aid.
A 2017 poll found that 59% of Americans said the U.S. spends too much on foreign aid, and in other polls it has been as low as 49%.
The 2015 Kaiser poll asked whether the United States spends too much on foreign aid, and 56% of respondents said that it does.
When respondents to the 2015 Kaiser poll were told that less than 1% of the federal budget is for foreign aid, the number who thought the U.S. spends too much dropped to 28%.
Other polls have asked what would be an appropriate percentage of the federal budget to go to foreign aid, and the median answer is 10%.
A majority of Americans think that the federal government is spending too much on foreign aid.

If the ratio of aid to gross national income increased by 1% above the average for the sample countries, annual real per capita growth increased by approximately 0.35%.
Aid increases economic growth, according to the findings of the economists.
Some aid initiatives have failed to promote economic growth.
One reason aid could slow economic growth is 'Dutch disease,' a term coined by The Economist.
Dutch disease describes a decline in the Dutch economy in the 1960s after natural gas was discovered in the North Sea.
In the Republic, Somalia, and Malawi, aid amounts to approximately a quarter of the national income.
Aid is close to 20% of national income for Liberia and Afghanistan.
At high levels, aid can cause a substantial Dutch disease effect.
The impact of aid depends on how it is used.
Aid that improves infrastructure, agricultural methods, and workforce skills enhances productivity.
Improved productivity from aid can lead to increased exports that may outweigh the Dutch disease problem.
For ten years after Mozambique's civil war ended in 1992, European nations gave an extraordinarily high level of aid to Mozambique.
Over those years, 40% of Mozambique's gross national income was foreign aid.
Almost half of the aid to Mozambique was debt relief, which could not be spent within Mozambique.
Aid to Mozambique was used to build roads, hospitals, and schools and to improve workforce skills.
Mozambique's real economic growth per capita averaged 5.5% per annum after the civil war.
High levels of aid to Botswana after independence in 1966, to Taiwan in the 1950s, and to Uganda in the 1990s were compatible with strong economic growth.
Dutch disease is not inevitable when countries receive high levels of aid.
U.S. and European agricultural subsidies are a significant barrier to the growth of export industries in developing countries.
Poor countries' climate and cheap labor give them a natural competitive advantage in agriculture.
Burkina Faso, Mali, Benin, and Chad rely on cotton as the only source of income for millions of peasant farmers.
Many West African cotton farmers support families on less than $2 a day.
West African cotton farmers produce cotton more cheaply and more ecologically sustainably than U.S. cotton growers.
In 2017, 1,195 U.S. cotton growers shared $663,893,746 in taxpayer-funded subsidies.
The average subsidy per U.S. cotton grower in 2017 was more than half a million dollars.
In some years, the value of U.S. cotton subsidies has exceeded the market value of the cotton produced by subsidized growers.
Moussa Doumbia, a cotton farmer in Mali, earned less than $300 a year for his labor.
Moussa Doumbia struggled to feed his children and buy medicine for them.
Moussa Doumbia did not know he was getting less for his cotton because of U.S. subsidies to American cotton growers.
Daniel Sumner calculated that ending U.S. cotton subsidies would raise a West African cotton grower's income enough to cover all health care costs for four children.
Eliminating all agricultural subsidies and reducing nonagricultural tariffs by 50% would result in a global economic gain of at least $96 billion annually.
Of the $96 billion global economic gain, $30 billion would go to the developing world.
Eliminating agricultural subsidies would save U.S. taxpayers more than $16 billion per year.
Eliminating agricultural subsidies would save European taxpayers even more than $16 billion per year.
U.S. agricultural subsidies are authorized by Farm Bills, which are renewed every six years.
In 2008, opposition to U.S. agricultural subsidies united conservatives and liberals.
President George W. Bush described the 2008 Farm Bill as 'bloated and wasteful' and vetoed it.
Congress overrode President Bush's veto of the 2008 Farm Bill with a two-thirds majority.
When Congress stripped a subsidy from the 2014 Farm Bill, two new subsidies replaced it: Price Loss Coverage and Agriculture Risk Coverage.
The Price Loss Coverage and Agriculture Risk Coverage subsidies favor wealthier U.S. farms, including wealthy cotton growers.
President Donald Trump has proposed subsidy cuts, but Congress is likely to ignore the president's suggestion.
Less unfair trade rules would help, but would not guarantee that trade would lift every region out of poverty.
Economic growth can bypass people, regions, and even entire countries.
A country's government may follow ill-advised economic policies or have politics, customs, and social structures inimical to economic productivity.
Aid can be made conditional on policy reform in countries with poor economic policies.
Desire for growth is motivated by saving lives, reducing misery, and meeting people's basic needs.
Experts emphasize the importance of good institutions and practices in explaining why some nations are rich and others are poor.
Good institutions include the rule of law, protection of property rights, effective government, social conventions that enable trust, universal schooling, and low tolerance of corruption.
Effective government means the public sector works tolerably well.
In an effective government, starting a business does not require bribing officials.
In an effective government, rights as workers, consumers, and residents are protected from unsafe workplaces, unsafe products, and industrial pollution.
The rule of law protects people from violence and allows them to plan for the future with reasonable confidence that their property will not be taken.
The rule of law enables people to make contracts, knowing that breaches will be penalized.
A certain level of trust makes it easier for people to work together and creates a sense of community.
The idea that good institutions reduce poverty leads to making aid conditional on recipient governments providing conditions for economic growth.
In 2002, President George W. Bush set up the Millennium Challenge Account to reserve a portion of U.S. aid for governments that govern justly, invest in their people, and encourage economic freedom.
The Millennium Challenge Corporation was established to administer the Millennium Challenge Account.
The Millennium Challenge Corporation continued throughout the Obama administration.
The Millennium Challenge Corporation is the only sector of the U.S. aid program that has received favorable attention from the Trump administration.
The Millennium Challenge Corporation has been criticized for using aid to spread the capitalist model of development.

The conditions for eligibility for Millennium Challenge Corporation aid have been credited with successes such as improvements in Liberia's educational data, anti-corruption efforts in Sierra Leone, and sales of land in the Senegal River Valley to women.

A study by the Center for Global Development found that in African countries with a Millennium Challenge Corporation compact, U.S. aid programs had a dramatically higher alignment with citizens' priorities than in countries without a compact.
Paul Collier has demonstrated that aid can be effective in improving institutions, especially in fragile states.
Countries emerging from civil war are at high risk of falling back into conflict.
Collier has shown that substantial, properly directed, and sustained aid can enhance governments' capacity to avoid returning to conflict.
Mozambique and Sierra Leone are examples where aid has made a difference after internal war.
Opportunities arise when a reforming government replaces a corrupt or incompetent regime with a more honest and capable one.
Levy Mwanawasa's government in Zambia succeeded an extremely corrupt government in 2002.
Collier found that providing $1 billion of technical assistance over four years could produce $15 billion worth of economic benefits to a country with a reforming government.
The $15 billion benefit does not include the gain to the world from countries having effective governments.
Making aid conditional on reform can help improve corrupt or inefficient governments and avoid conflict.
Sometimes conditions are so bad that nothing can diminish the misery of a bad government's citizens.
At other times, aid can directly help the poorest and make a significant and sustainable difference, even if it does not lead to better institutions.
In cases where aid can help the poorest directly, it should not be withheld.
The story of microfinance began in 1976 with Muhammad Yunus, then head of the economics department at Chittagong University in Bangladesh.
Yunus found that women in Jobra village had to borrow from local moneylenders at high interest rates to buy bamboo for making furniture.
The high interest rates charged by moneylenders kept the women in poverty.
Yunus lent US$27 from his own pocket to a group of 42 women in Jobra village.
The small loan of about 64 cents per person helped the women become independent from moneylenders and eventually repay the loan.
Yunus persuaded a government bank to fund a pilot project making very small loans to villagers.
Over six years, the pilot project made thousands of loans, usually to groups of women.
The women knew that if they did not repay the loans, others in the group would not be able to borrow.
Virtually all the loans in the pilot project were repaid.
This experience reversed the then-accepted economic wisdom that lending to the poor is high risk and only viable with high interest rates.
In 1982, Yunus founded the Grameen Bank to provide loans across Bangladesh.
Researchers from Innovations for Poverty Action and the Jameel Poverty Action Lab conducted six separate studies of microcredit.
The studies concluded that small, short-term loans generally do not lead to increased income for poor borrowers.
The studies found that microcredit does not lead to increased investments in children's schooling for poor borrowers.
The studies found that microcredit does not result in substantial gains in women's empowerment for poor borrowers.
Making loans available to poor people can help them deal with emergencies.
Microcredit can help poor people feed their families in lean times.
Microcredit does not transform the lives of borrowers.
Microcredit does not make a major contribution to ending poverty.
Charities are often started by founders who care about a problem and have an idea about how to solve it.
Charity founders may try their solution in one location and, if it helps, seek to scale it up.
Charities gain support from donors who care about the issue and believe in the strategy.
It is difficult for charity founders to be objective in assessing the success of their project.
Evidence Action is a nonprofit recommended by The Life You Can Save.
Evidence Action runs large-scale programs and a 'Beta' incubator to test promising interventions.
The Beta incubator assesses impact, cost-effectiveness, and scalability before scaling up interventions.
No Lean Season was a program in Evidence Action's Beta incubator.
No Lean Season was designed to address a drop-off in work opportunities for ultra-poor rural laborers during the period between planting and harvesting crops.
Lean season poverty affects 600 million people globally.
The idea behind No Lean Season was to provide small travel subsidies or loans to enable laborers to find jobs in other areas during the lean season.
Small-scale randomized controlled trials in Northern Bangladesh showed positive impacts on income and consumption for families participating in No Lean Season.
GiveWell named No Lean Season a Top Charity for 2017.
Evidence Action continues to test its programs as they increase in scale.
Evidence Action collaborated with leading economists to conduct a large-scale randomized controlled trial of No Lean Season.
The large-scale trial found that fewer workers took up the loans in No Lean Season.
The large-scale trial found that No Lean Season had no impact on inducing migration, income, or consumption.
Evidence Action informed GiveWell that No Lean Season should not be named a Top Charity for 2018.
Evidence Action stopped raising funds for No Lean Season while conducting further research.
Evidence Action found evidence that proper financial procedures had not always been followed by their local partner organization.
After further investigation, Evidence Action decided to end the No Lean Season program entirely.
Evidence Action's transparency and honesty has made it a model for evidence-based organizations.
Evidence Action's CEO Kanika Bahl stated that organizations must be willing to make tough calls and exit programs when appropriate.
Bahl stated that NGOs should not walk away from work that measurably improves lives just because a program faces challenges.
Bahl stated that in high-challenge settings, NGOs must cost-effectively and responsibly mitigate risks.
Flaws in one of Evidence Action's previously lauded programs have enhanced, not diminished, the organization's reputation.
If more charities follow Evidence Action's lead and more donors reward honest reporting, more resources will flow to effective programs.
The Millennium Villages Project was launched in 2005 by the United Nations Millennium Project, directed by Jeffrey Sachs.
The Millennium Villages Project aimed to assist villages in ten Sub-Saharan African countries over ten years.
The Project used a combination of interventions in agriculture, nutrition, education, health, and infrastructure.
The underlying hypothesis of the Project was that a combination of interventions would enable villagers to escape poverty.
The Millennium Villages Project attracted support from high-profile individuals including Madonna, Bono, Angelina Jolie, Brad Pitt, and George Soros.
The Project did not enable the villages to achieve the Millennium Development Goals.
The initial promise of the Project was not fulfilled.
The Project was not more rigorously evaluated.
Transparency and a rigorous approach to project planning, execution, and evidence collection should be a priority in all new approaches to aid.
The Graduation approach is a multifaceted program that has been more rigorously evaluated than the Project.
The Graduation approach provides an asset, either cash to start a business or a productive asset such as chickens.
The Graduation approach includes training in how to use the asset to generate income.
The Graduation approach provides mentoring for the three-year duration of the project.
The Graduation approach includes access to a savings and loan facility or group.
Randomized controlled trials were used to evaluate the Graduation approach in six different countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
The trials showed sustained income increases in five of the six countries.
The trials showed increases in consumption for families who had been so poor that they were missing meals.
Village Enterprise used the Graduation approach in Kenya and Uganda.
Village Enterprise invited Innovations for Poverty Action to conduct a large-scale randomized controlled trial of their one-year version of the program.
The trial found sustained positive outcomes, including improvements in nutrition and subjective well-being.
At the time of writing, there have been nine well-conducted randomized controlled trials of the Graduation approach.
The combination of providing cash or an in-kind asset, business training, and savings groups is effective in improving the position of extremely poor people.
A World Bank Brief suggests the Graduation approach can be an integral component of strategies aimed at eradicating extreme poverty.
Village Enterprise specializes in starting business enterprises in villages.
Since 1987, Village Enterprise has helped start over 44,700 businesses and trained more than 175,000 East Africans.
Village Enterprise employs almost entirely local East African staff.
Village Enterprise underwent an independent impact audit by ImpactMatters.
ImpactMatters gave Village Enterprise a five star rating, the highest possible, across all categories.
ImpactMatters estimated a return of $1.80 of lifetime household income for every $1 spent by Village Enterprise.
Village Enterprise estimates its program costs about $595 per three-person business.
Each new business started by Village Enterprise improves the standard of living for approximately 20 individuals, based on the average family size in the region.
If Village Enterprise's estimates are correct, lives are improved for an impressively modest $30 per person.
Further research will show whether effectiveness can be sustained when these programs are conducted on a much larger scale.
To learn what works and what does not work, the most objective possible means of assessing programs must be used.
Ideally, randomized controlled trials should be announced before they are carried out and have results and methods completely open to public scrutiny.
When evidence of what works on a small scale is available, it can be tried on a larger scale while continuing to assess the intervention.
The Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) was founded at MIT by Esther Duflo.
J-PAL pioneered the use of randomized controlled trials to assess programs to assist people in poverty.
Innovations for Poverty Action was set up by Dean Karlan, who studied under Duflo and became a professor of economics at Yale University.
J-PAL and Innovations for Poverty Action have been involved in assessing interventions such as microcredit programs and the Graduation approach.
J-PAL and Innovations for Poverty Action research interventions, whereas GiveWell researches charities.
The strong evidence bases of many of GiveWell's and The Life You Can Save's recommended charities derive from rigorous studies by J-PAL and Innovations for Poverty Action.
There is insufficient capacity to assess all interventions that need to be evaluated.
GiveWell has announced plans to more than double its research staff to evaluate interventions that are harder to measure, including opportunities to influence government policy.
D-Rev is a nonprofit design firm currently recommended by The Life You Can Save.
In many affluent countries, treating mental illness is extremely cost-effective.
Treating mental illness improves well-being and increases productivity.
Mental illness is a cause of unemployment, absenteeism, and poor workplace performance.
A study of 15 European countries estimated the economic cost of mental illness at 3–4% of gross national product.
There is no reason to think that mental illness is less of a problem in low-income countries.
Few people in low-income countries have access to any form of counselling or treatment for mental illness.
Since 2013, StrongMinds has treated depression in African women.
StrongMinds uses group therapy, a low-cost method adapted to local culture and delivered by specially trained local women.
Initial studies show that 75% of participating women remain depression-free six months after StrongMinds treatment ends.
StrongMinds is seeking to scale up its group therapy method.
StrongMinds' vision is that every African woman suffering from depression will be able to take part in therapy.
A project in Pune, India, assisted ragpickers who make their living by collecting recyclables from the town garbage dump.
Ragpickers in Pune were paid one rupee (about three cents) for a kilogram of plastic.
Ragpickers in Pune are from the Dalit caste, formerly known as Untouchables.
Dalit ragpickers had been isolated, held in contempt, exploited economically, and sexually harassed by dealers.
Laxmi Narayan, a lecturer in adult education, ran a literacy program for ragpickers in Pune.
Laxmi Narayan sought and gained assistance from Oxfam to help the women organize into the Registered Association of Ragpickers.
The Registered Association of Ragpickers enabled members to demand better prices and protected them from harassment.
The association persuaded the Pune Municipal Council to issue ragpickers identity cards for entry to apartment buildings.
Residents in Pune were asked to separate their recyclables for collection by ragpickers.
Many ragpickers were able to work in clean and safe conditions by collecting recyclables directly from homes.
Some ragpickers still worked in the dumps but benefited from new protections.
The association began running a savings scheme and a microcredit facility.
Interest earned on pooled savings was used to provide scholarships and school texts for members' children.
Previously, small children had worked alongside their mothers in the city dump.
Most ragpickers now realize that by going to school, their children might enjoy opportunities they did not have.
The Registered Association of Ragpickers became self-supporting and did not require further support from Oxfam.
Oxfam is an advocate for policy change as well as direct aid projects.
Mozambique has a population of 30 million, 63% of whom live on less than $1.90 per day.
Women in Mozambique are especially at risk of living in extreme poverty.
According to traditional law in Mozambique, if a woman's husband died, the couple's home and land belonged to his family.
Divorced women in Mozambique had no claim to property and were often left penniless.
Fathers who left their families in Mozambique had no legal obligation to support their children.
In the 1990s, women in Mozambique organized a coalition to end these injustices.
Oxfam provided technical support and advocacy training to Mozambican women's organizations.
Oxfam helped organizations from different parts of Mozambique to meet and work together.
Oxfam supported a media campaign in Mozambique involving television, radio, newspapers, and street theater.
The campaign in Mozambique won support in many sectors of society and government.
In 2004, Mozambique's national parliament passed a new family law requiring men to support women pregnant with their child and to pay child support after birth.
The new family law in Mozambique granted women rights over the couple's property after one year of living together in a customary marriage.
In 2014, Ghana's budget allocated $116 million, or 15% of the government's oil revenues, to agriculture.
Most of the $116 million allocated to agriculture in Ghana in 2014 was directed at 'poverty-focused agriculture' to benefit smallholder farmers.
Oil revenue in Ghana was used to build a dam that provides water for 75 families cultivating small plots of land in the country's arid northeast.
Since 2014, Oxfam has continued to support Ghanaian organizations that monitor how oil revenue is spent.
Oxfam's expenditure on the campaign, including staff time, was no more than $200,000.
Oxfam paid further modest sums to local monitoring organizations in Ghana.
It is possible that the Ghanaian government would have reached the same outcome without Oxfam's involvement.
If Oxfam's interventions made it only 1% more likely that a significant portion of oil revenue would help Ghanaians in extreme poverty, the expected value of Oxfam's actions would be $1.16 million.
Similar cost/benefit ratios to Oxfam's Ghana campaign are likely in future years.
Even if most advocacy campaigns fail, one large success can offset many losses.
There is much to learn about how best to help people in extreme poverty.
Knowledge about how to help people in extreme poverty is increasing over time.
Being open about mistakes allows knowledge about poverty alleviation to continue to grow.
Changes in government aid policies could make a big difference in helping people in extreme poverty.
Not subsidizing wealthy producers who can undercut small peasant farmers in low-income countries is a suggested change in aid policy.
Not tying aid to purchasing products domestically and exporting them on national carriers is another suggested change in aid policy.
Not using aid to advance national political agendas is a further suggested change in aid policy.
When government aid is focused on helping people in extreme poverty, it can be effective.
If aid is used to enhance productivity, it can lead to increased exports that offset the potential 'Dutch disease' effect of large aid inflows.
Aid can be valuable for improving institutions.
Putting conditions on aid is a legitimate way to improve institutions.
Aid can play an important role in helping a country heal after an internal conflict.
There are differences between government aid and individual aid.
Individuals can choose where they donate.
By choosing where to donate, individuals can have a big impact in extending the work of effective organizations.
The question of how much individuals ought to give remains unresolved.
Obligations to family and the giving habits of those around us complicate the question of how much to give.
Charlotte Perkins Gilman's short story 'The Unnatural Mother' was first published in 1895.
In 'The Unnatural Mother,' Esther Greenwood chooses to warn villagers of a dam giving way rather than save her own child first.
Esther Greenwood saves the villagers and then returns for her child, but drowns in the attempt.
Esther Greenwood's child survives despite her drowning.
Old Mrs. Briggs calls Esther an 'unnatural mother' for not putting her own child's life ahead of others.
Mrs. Briggs's daughter, Mary Amelia, points out that Esther saved 1,500 lives.
Mrs. Briggs is ashamed of Mary Amelia for expressing the opinion that Esther did the right thing.
The story raises questions about a parent's duty in extreme circumstances.
It is both wrong and unnatural not to love one's own children.
Parents must provide for their children's needs, including feeding, housing, clothing, and educating them.
Few people will ever face the question of whether to put their own child's life at risk to save hundreds of others.
A real dilemma for many is whether it is wrong to deny children luxuries in order to donate savings to help strangers.
Zell Kravinsky has struggled with the dilemma of obligations to family versus strangers.
Most people put their obligations to their family, especially their children, above everything else.
Putting the family first feels natural and, in most cases, right to most people.
Kravinsky sees the sacrosanct commitment to the family as a rationalization for greed and selfishness.
Kravinsky claims that people often justify working for companies they dislike by saying they are doing it for their children.
Kravinsky tells students that the chance of dying as a result of donating a kidney is about 1 in 4,000.
Kravinsky argues that withholding a kidney from someone who would otherwise die means valuing your own life four thousand times more than that of a stranger.
Kravinsky describes the ratio of valuing one's own life four thousand times more than a stranger's as 'obscene.'
Some students question Kravinsky's facts and suggest the risks of kidney donation are higher than 1 in 4,000.
A study of kidney donors put the risk of dying around the time of surgery at 1 in 3,225.
Most deaths in the kidney donor study were for donors with hypertension.
Mortality for a kidney donor without hypertension was less than 1 in 7,500.
The study did not find long-term mortality to be higher in kidney donors than in matched non-donors.
Another group of researchers pooled data from 52 previous studies covering 118,426 donors to examine long-term health impacts of kidney donation.
The pooled study found that women who became pregnant after donating had a higher risk of preeclampsia.
All kidney donors had a higher risk of end-stage renal disease, but the absolute risk was still low.
The pooled study found no evidence of higher overall mortality or adverse psychosocial health outcomes for kidney donors.
The medical risks of playing NFL football are much greater, both near-term and long-term, than those of donating a kidney.
Success cannot be guaranteed for the recipient of a kidney, as 5% of those who receive a kidney from a living donor die within a year of the operation.
The 5% recipient mortality rate makes only a minor difference to the risk/benefit ratio of kidney donation.
Some students are open to questioning themselves about how much they value their own life compared to a stranger's.
Some students are comfortable valuing their own life more than four thousand times that of a stranger.
A few students begin to think seriously about donating a kidney after Kravinsky's presentation.
One student donated a kidney as a result of taking the author's online course on effective altruism.
Four other students' kidney donations were influenced by reading the author's work.
Paul Farmer is the cofounder of Partners in Health, an organization that brings modern medical science to those most in need.
Farmer feels a conflict between his love for his family and his concern for strangers.
Farmer spent a year in Haiti after college because he knew his money would go a long way there.
While volunteering at a Haitian hospital, Farmer befriended a young American doctor who was about to return to the United States.
The American doctor said he could not wait to leave Haiti because there was no electricity and conditions were brutal.
Farmer asked the American doctor if he was worried about not being able to forget the disease in Haiti.
The American doctor replied that he was an American and was going home.
Farmer wondered why being an American meant you could forget about people dying for lack of medical care in Haiti.
Farmer decided he would become a doctor after this experience.
Farmer began studying for his medical degree at Harvard in 1984.
Farmer regularly returned to Haiti to do research on public health problems in Cange.
Farmer met Tom White, a major Boston philanthropist, during this period.
Farmer brought White to Haiti, and White helped him start Partners in Health and became its principal financial backer in its formative years.
In 1993, the MacArthur Foundation awarded Farmer a 'genius grant' of $220,000.
Farmer donated the entire MacArthur grant to Partners in Health.
After completing his medical training, Farmer had appointments at Harvard in medical anthropology and at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston in infectious diseases.
Farmer carries with him a picture of his daughter Catherine and a picture of a Haitian child patient suffering from malnutrition.
Kidder accompanied Farmer when he visited his wife and child in Paris.
Didi, Farmer's wife, was studying the ordeals of her ancestors in the archives of the French slaveowners.
Farmer was playing with Catherine shortly after arriving in Paris.
Didi asked Farmer when he was leaving for Moscow, where Partners in Health was involved in an antituberculosis program.
Farmer replied that he was leaving the next morning.
Didi was clearly upset by Farmer's imminent departure.
Farmer covered his mouth with both hands in response to Didi's exclamation.
Kidder observed that it was the first time he had seen Farmer at a loss for words or action.
Farmer is driven by the thought that if he does not work hard, someone will die who does not have to.
Farmer cannot accept that people are dying of diseases for which treatments exist.
Farmer has said, 'One can never work overtime for the poor.'
Farmer believes, 'We're only scrambling to make up for our deficiencies.'
Kravinsky insists that he loves his children as much as any parent.
Kravinsky protected his children from his own commitment to others by setting up a trust fund for them.
Kravinsky does not believe his fatherly love justifies valuing his children's lives thousands of times more than the lives of strangers' children.
When pressed by Ian Parker to calculate a ratio between his love for his children and for unknown children, Kravinsky said he would not let many children die so his kids could live.
Kravinsky stated, 'I don't think that two kids should die so that one of my kids has comfort, and I don't know that two children should die so that one of my kids lives.'
MIT philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson commented that a father who says he is no more concerned about his children's lives than about anybody else's is a defective parent.
Kravinsky did not say he is no more concerned about his children's lives than anybody else's, but he came closer to that than most people would.
Children need loving parents who will protect them and stick by them.
Children might be disturbed to discover that their father would allow them to die so that the children of strangers could be saved.
Literature contains situations where parents must choose between their child and a broader moral imperative.
Abraham is honored in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic religions for his readiness to obey God's command to sacrifice his son Isaac.
The ancient Greeks considered that a father might have to sacrifice a child for a greater good.
In Euripides' play Iphigeneia at Aulis, Agamemnon is compelled to sacrifice his daughter Iphigeneia so the Greek fleet can sail for Troy.
Agamemnon tells his daughter that Greece compels him to sacrifice her, whatever he wishes.
Agamemnon's act is treated with more skepticism in classical literature than Abraham's in Genesis.
The ancient Greeks did not think pursuing the Trojan War was as important as the writers of the Bible thought obeying God was.
Joseph Kanon's novel The Good German explores the limits of what a mother may do to save her child.
Renate Naumann, a German Jewish woman, is on trial for collaborating with the Nazis as a Greifer in The Good German.
If Naumann had refused or failed to meet her quota, her own life and that of her elderly mother would have been at risk.
Naumann has a son who could not have survived without her collaboration.
The text questions whether Naumann's collaboration is acceptable because it saved her son.
The text suggests we tend to blame people more for their acts than for their omissions.
We are more ready to condemn Naumann for saving her child than to denounce a woman who saves her own child at the cost of failing to warn others.
Condemning Naumann puts limits on what one may do to save one's own child.
Neither Esther Greenwood, Zell Kravinsky, nor Paul Farmer is considered a defective parent in the text.
Farmer, Kravinsky, and Greenwood are described as being pulled by the needs of others in a way most people are not.
Kravinsky eventually returned to real estate, made more money, and bought his family a larger home.
He does not spend money on luxuries.
He does not express disapproval of those who spend money on luxuries, as long as they also give something to the poor.
Jim Kim told Tracy Kidder that people should be inspired by Paul, but it is unrealistic to expect everyone to be like him.
Jim Kim said that if the poor have to wait for many people like Paul to come along before they get good health care, they are totally fucked.
The text suggests that standards may need to be set lower to draw more people to meet them.
Chuck Collins is the great-grandson of Oscar Mayer, founder of the hot dog producer.
Chuck Collins was born into the wealthiest 1% of Americans.
At 16, Chuck Collins was told he would inherit a share of the Mayer family fortune.
Chuck Collins grew up in an affluent suburb of Detroit.
Chuck Collins was aware that others in Detroit were leading very different lives and felt the unfairness of it.
Chuck Collins gave away most of his wealth before he had children.
People told Chuck Collins that he should not be reckless with his children's future by giving away his wealth.
Chuck Collins responded that parents make decisions for their children all the time, including deciding not to leave them an inheritance.
Chuck Collins said his kids grew up with advantages such as intergenerational stability, access to education, financial literacy, and being white, but they will not get an inheritance.
Chuck Collins believes that inherited wealth is not good for children.
Chuck Collins co-founded Responsible Wealth, an organization for people in the richest 5% of wealth or income in the United States that campaigns for tax fairness.
Responsible Wealth campaigns for higher taxes on the incomes of the wealthy.
Chuck Collins is now a Senior Scholar at the Institute for Policy Studies.
Chuck Collins directs the Institute's Program on Inequality and the Common Good.
Chuck Collins co-authored 'Wealth and our Commonwealth' with Bill Gates Sr.
'Wealth and our Commonwealth' makes the case for taxing inherited fortunes.
Chuck Collins accepts the argument that people must respond to the needs of their immediate family.
Chuck Collins adds that once one's immediate family is okay, the circle of concern should be expanded.
Chuck Collins says that a larger sense of family is a radical idea, but society gets into trouble when people do not see that they are in the same boat.
The notion of when one's family is 'okay' is described as very vague.
Students often ask whether their parents are wrong to send them to expensive universities like Princeton.
The estimated cost for attending Princeton in 2019–20 is $73,450 if no financial aid is received.
